turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, Doc, I'm here because... honestly, I just can't seem to stop moving. It’s hard to explain exactly, but it’s like I’ve got this motor running inside me all day long. Just constantly revving, you know? From the minute I open my eyes, it's just humming away, and it never really shuts off. 

And it's a real problem because if I have to sit still anywhere, I just can't do it. Like at church, for instance. I try to sit in the pew and just listen to the sermon, but after a few minutes, I start feeling completely trapped. I get this tight, awful feeling, and I just have to get up and walk to the back or go to the bathroom just to do something, anything, to keep moving. 

It was the exact same thing out there in your clinic waiting room just now. The lady up front told me to have a seat, and I think I made it about two minutes before I was up pacing around the chairs and looking at the posters on the walls. I just couldn't stay in the chair. And it's like that at home, too. I can't even sit through a whole meal or watch a TV show without feeling boxed in. I just feel trapped all the time if I'm not moving, and I always have to get up and find something to do. It's driving me crazy, just having this engine going all the time and not being able to just sit and relax like a normal person.

turns.doctor_question: When you're sitting still and feel that urge to move, is it more like you physically can't control the urge to move, or is it more like you feel anxious or panicky about being trapped and need to escape that feeling?
turns.patient_response:
Well, Doc, honestly... I don't rightly know how to split the two up, if I'm being completely honest with you. It's not like... I mean, I don't think I'm having a panic attack or nothing like that. I'm not scared of the chair, you know? But it’s just this... this massive build-up. 

Like, okay, say I'm sitting there, right? First, my leg usually starts bouncing. I don't even tell it to bounce, it just starts going a mile a minute all on its own. And then I realize it's bouncing, and I try to press my foot down flat on the floor to make it stop because I know it annoys people. But when I do that, the feeling just moves up into my chest and my arms, and it's like this pressure, this really tight, uncomfortable pressure, just building and building and building. 

So, is it my body doing it or my head? I really couldn't tell you. It’s just like my whole system is screaming at me that sitting still is the absolute wrong thing to be doing right at that exact second. And yeah, I guess I do feel trapped, but not like... not like a claustrophobia kind of trapped where I'm scared of the room shrinking or the doors locking. It's more like I'm trapped inside my own skin, if that makes any sense at all? Like my skin is just too tight and the only way to loosen it up is to get up and walk around. 

I remember a couple weeks ago, my sister made me sit down at her kitchen table to help her sort out some mail, and I swear to you, I lasted maybe five minutes before I felt that exact thing. My knee was going, my hands were tapping the table, and she’s telling me to just sit still, but all I could think was, "If I don't stand up right now, I'm gonna jump straight out of my own body." So I don't know if that's me physically not being able to control my muscles or me just mentally needing to escape that awful tight feeling. It's just... it's just all of it at once, all tangled up together, and I just know I gotta get up. I've never really thought about whether it's an anxious thing or a physical thing, it's just what happens every single time.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient describes their leg bouncing 'a mile a minute' and their hands tapping the table.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes an intense internal feeling of restlessness, stating they feel 'trapped inside my own skin' and like they are going to 'jump straight out of my own body' if they don't stand up.

turns.doctor_question: How long have you been experiencing this constant need to move and inability to sit still? Has it been going on your whole life, or did it start at some point?
turns.patient_response:
Well, Doc, that's a good question, and honestly, if I really sit down and think about it... well, I mean, I guess I've always been a little antsy, you know? Never been the type to just sit around doing nothing. But this? This feeling like my skin is crawling and I'm gonna explode if I don't get up? That hasn't been forever. 

I can actually pinpoint it pretty well. It's been about... well, let's see, it was right around the time the weather started turning cold two years ago. Yeah, so maybe two years and two months, right around there. And the reason I know that is because that's when my uncle—he's the one who raised me mostly—he took a real bad turn with his health. He had this stroke, out of nowhere, just sitting in his favorite recliner watching the game, and boom. Next thing we know, he's in the hospital for weeks, and then he comes home and he can't do hardly anything for himself anymore. 

And, well, since I'm not working right now, it fell on me to step up. Which is fine, he's family, I'd do anything for him. But man, it was a lot all at once. Suddenly I'm the one having to make sure his meds are sorted, helping him get to the bathroom, keeping the house clean, running to the pharmacy, dealing with the insurance people on the phone—which is a whole other nightmare, let me tell you, they put you on hold for an hour and expect you to just sit there. 

And I think... I think that's when this motor inside me really got cranked up to high gear and the knob broke off. Because before that, if I got antsy, I'd just go outside and tinker with my truck or walk down to the corner store. But suddenly, I couldn't just leave whenever I wanted. I had to be there, in the house, on call basically. I had to sit by his bed while he slept just in case he woke up and needed something. And that's when it got unbearable. That's when I started feeling that tight pressure in my chest and my legs bouncing out of control. It’s like, the more I had to sit still and be responsible, the more my body just refused to cooperate. And it's just been like that ever since, every single day for the last two years and a couple of months. Just non-stop.

turns.doctor_question: Before this started two years ago, were you someone who worried a lot or felt anxious about things in general? Or did the worrying and anxiety really only start around the same time as this restless feeling?
turns.patient_response:
Well, Doc... no, not really. I mean, if I really think on it... no. I was never much of a worrier before all this happened. People actually used to tell me I was too laid back, if you can believe it, considering how I am right now. 

Like, back in the day, I'd just kind of take things as they come. I never finished high school, you know, left in the middle of eighth grade, so I always just worked with my hands, doing odd jobs, landscaping, fixing up cars, whatever paid cash. And if work dried up for a week or two, or if I was short on rent, it didn't keep me up at night. I didn't sit around chewing my fingernails about what might happen tomorrow. I just figured, well, something will turn up. Like my buddy Dave, he used to get all worked up about every little thing—if his truck made a funny noise, he'd be sweating bullets thinking the transmission was gonna drop right there on the highway. But me? I'd just turn the radio up louder and keep driving until it actually broke down. That was just my way. I didn't borrow trouble, as my uncle used to say.

So, no, I didn't have all this... this heavy worry and this buzzing feeling back then. It really wasn't until the stroke. Because suddenly, it wasn't just me I was looking out for, right? If my truck breaks down, who cares, I walk. But if I mess up his pills, or if I don't hear him calling out from the bedroom because I'm out in the yard messing with some tools... well, that's a whole different ballgame. That's serious. 

So yeah, the worrying really kicked off right exactly when this whole motor-running-in-my-chest thing started. Before that, I was just... I was just doing my thing, not stressing. But now it's like my brain and my body are just constantly waiting for something terrible to happen, and I can't shut it off. Like I was saying about your waiting room out there, I just sit down and my head starts going, and my legs start going, and it's like if I don't get up and pace, I'm gonna miss something or do something wrong. It's just exhausting, Doc, it really is, never having a minute of peace where I can just sit and be still like I used to.

turns.doctor_question: How is your uncle doing now, two years later? Is he still living with you and still requiring that same level of care and attention from you?
turns.patient_response:
Well, Doc, yeah... yeah, he’s still with me. Still in the same house. We actually... well, we had to move his bed downstairs into what used to be the dining room, because getting him up those narrow stairs was just a disaster waiting to happen. I mean, I remember this one time, maybe six months after he got back from the hospital, I was trying to help him up the steps and my foot slipped, and I swear my heart almost jumped straight out of my throat. So, yeah, the dining room is his bedroom now. 

And as for how he’s doing... I mean, he’s alive, right? But it’s not like he bounced back to how he was before the stroke. He still can’t really use his left arm or leg much at all. He just sits in his recliner—we actually had to get a new one, one of those mechanical lift chairs that kind of tips you forward on an angle? Because otherwise I was pulling my shoulder out trying to haul him up every single time he needed to use the bathroom. 

And the care... man, it’s just as much, if not more, if I’m being completely honest. Because now he gets frustrated, you know? He used to be this big, tough guy, worked his whole life, and now he has to ask me to get him a glass of water or pick up the TV remote if he drops it. So he gets cranky, and I get antsy, and we just kind of bounce off each other all day. I’m still doing all his meals, sorting all his meds... and they just changed his pills again, which means another half hour on the phone with the pharmacy where I'm just pacing circles in the kitchen while that awful hold music plays. 

So yeah, I’m still on duty basically twenty-four-seven. I don’t get a day off. If I need to go to the grocery store, I have to wait until my sister can come over and sit with him, and even then, I’m literally running through the aisles like my shoes are on fire because I just have this feeling he’s gonna need something the second I’m not there. So it hasn't let up one bit, Doc. Not one bit.

turns.doctor_question: When you're sitting still and feeling that tight pressure building up in your chest and legs, are you also having racing thoughts or worries running through your mind at the same time? turns.patient_response:
Well, Doc, I... I really don't know if I can separate the two, if I'm being completely honest. I've never really stopped to think about what my brain is doing while my body is throwing a fit. 

Like, okay, take the other night for example. We're sitting in the living room, and my uncle is dozing off in his lift chair while one of his old Westerns is on the TV—he watches those same episodes of Gunsmoke over and over, I swear I know all the words by now. But anyway, I'm sitting on the edge of the couch, just trying to be quiet so I don't wake him up, right? And that's when it starts. That tight feeling in my chest, and my right heel just starts going. Tap, tap, tap on the floorboards, like a jackhammer. 

And you're asking if my mind is racing with worries right then? I... I don't think so? I mean, I don't think I'm sitting there sweating over the electric bill or what the insurance company is gonna say next. It’s not like my brain is flipping through some big list of bad things that could happen. I haven't really noticed any specific thoughts like that. 

It's more like... well, my mind definitely isn't calm, but that's just because my body is so loud, you know what I mean? How can your head be peaceful when your chest feels like a shaken-up can of soda that's about to pop? I don't think I'm actually worrying about anything in those exact moments. I'm just so hyper-focused on how incredibly bad I need to stand up. It's like my brain is just static, just this loud buzzing noise telling my legs to move, move, move. So I end up getting up and just pacing around the kitchen island, tracing the grout lines in the tile, not really thinking about a single thing other than just walking off that awful pressure. So, yeah, I'm not really sure what my thoughts are doing, because I'm not really thinking at all, just... just reacting to my body, I guess.

turns.patient_response:
Well, Doc, pills? For me? No, no way. I mean, I don't take anything at all. I eat whatever's around, I keep moving... I mean, my body works totally fine. It's really just this... this engine inside my chest that won't shut off, like we were talking about. 

But no actual diseases or anything. I mean, if my thyroid was messed up, wouldn't I be tired and sluggish all the time? I'm the exact opposite of sluggish. turns.doctor_question: Have you been drinking more alcohol than usual in the past two years, or using any other substances like marijuana, cocaine, or anything else to help you cope with the stress?
turns.patient_response:
Well, Doc, it’s funny you ask that, because I know people always assume that when you’re stressed out of your mind, you just naturally hit the bottle, right? Like in those movies where the guy has a bad day and just pours himself this massive glass of whiskey. But for me? No. No, not at all. 

I mean, think about it—I’m on duty twenty-four-seven with my uncle. If I throw back a six-pack and pass out on the couch, what happens if he tries to get up to use the bathroom and takes a spill? I can’t be out cold, or even just, you know, buzzed and slow. I have to be ready to jump up the second he calls my name or drops his remote. And honestly, even before all this with him, alcohol just never really did it for me. It makes my head feel all fuzzy and heavy, and like I said, my body is always going a hundred miles an hour. It’s like trying to pour thick syrup into a race car engine—it just clashes, you know? I hate that feeling of being weighed down. 

And as for the other stuff... marijuana, cocaine? Man, no way. Absolutely not. First off, I wouldn't even know where to get anything like that even if I wanted it, which I don't. I barely leave the house! Like I told you, I’m literally sprinting through the grocery store aisles just trying to buy milk and bread before my sister has to leave. When am I gonna have time to go track down some guy selling drugs? 

Plus, if you think about it, with how fast my chest is always buzzing and how tight everything feels with this... this restless pressure thing... if I took something like cocaine that’s supposed to amp you up even more? Holy cow, Doc, I think my heart would just explode. I’d probably vibrate right through the floorboards into the basement. And weed? My buddy Dave—the guy with the bad knee I was telling you about—he smokes that stuff sometimes, and he just melts into his couch eating potato chips for three hours straight. I can’t even sit still for three minutes! I'd probably go crazy feeling trapped in my own body like that. 

So no, none of that. I don't touch any of it. I mean, I drink coffee, sure, maybe a pot or two a day just because it gives my hands something to do while I'm pacing the kitchen waiting on hold with the pharmacy, but that's just normal grocery store coffee, you know? No booze, no drugs, nothing like that to cope. Just me dealing with it on my own.

turns.doctor_question: Besides this restless, tight feeling in your chest and the need to move around, do you experience other things like sudden waves of fear or panic, or do you find yourself worrying a lot about things that might go wrong—like with your uncle's health, or money, or other situations?
turns.patient_response:
Well, Doc, panic? Like, out of nowhere? No, I don't think so. When you say panic, I picture those people in the movies who have to breathe into a brown paper bag, you know? Like they're hyperventilating and think the world is ending or the sky is falling. I don't get anything like that at all. 

And the worrying part... it's kind of exactly like I was saying before about my thoughts. I just don't sit around dwelling on stuff. Like with my uncle's health, right? He's old. He's got a bad ticker, he's got bad joints, things are gonna go wrong, that's just a fact of life. My sister, she's the worrier in the family. She'll call me up on a Tuesday afternoon and talk for forty-five minutes straight about, oh, what if his Medicare doesn't cover the repairs on his lift chair, or what if he tries to get up to get a glass of water while I'm in the bathroom and he breaks his hip? And she gets herself all worked up, practically crying on the phone, stressing over every little detail of what might happen next month or next year. 

But me? I'm usually just walking laps around the kitchen island while she's talking on speakerphone, just tapping my fingers on the counter, waiting for her to finish so I can go fix the squeaky hinge on the back screen door or go rake the gravel in the driveway. I don't actually feel that worry she has. It's like my brain just doesn't hold onto those kinds of thoughts long enough to actually get scared about them. If something happens, it happens, and I'll deal with it right then and there. I literally don't have the attention span to sit on the couch and stew on a bunch of what-ifs. 

It's the exact same deal with money. We don't have a lot of it, obviously. I haven't worked a real paycheck job since I had to move in here full-time to watch him, so we're just scraping by on his disability checks and whatever my sister chips in. But I don't lay in bed at night staring at the ceiling calculating pennies and sweating over the electric bill. I lay in bed staring at the ceiling because my legs feel like they're plugged into a wall socket and I feel like I need to go sprint down the street in the pitch black. 

So, yeah, it's never fear, and it's never really worrying about the future or money or what's gonna happen to him. I don't get those waves of panic. It's always just right now, this exact second, my chest is tight and my body is screaming at me to get up and move. That's really all it ever is.

I'll be laying there, staring at the ceiling fan—I count the little ridges on the blades sometimes, or watch the shadows from the streetlamp, just to give my eyes something to do—and my legs, man, they just start... buzzing. Like a low-grade hum right deep down in the bones. And I'll try to just lay still, I really will. I'll grip the edge of the mattress and tell myself, "Just go to sleep, man, you gotta be up to make his oatmeal in three hours anyway," but then my knee just starts bouncing under the blanket on its own. There's no worry. There's no picture in my head of something bad happening. It's just... energy. This crazy, trapped energy. It gets so bad I just have to throw the covers off and get up, because if I stay in that bed one more second, I feel like my skin is gonna crawl right off my muscles. Half the time I end up pacing the hallway at three in the morning, or I'll go down to the basement and reorganize my uncle's old toolbox for the fifth time this month. I'll just sit there sorting the Phillips head screws from the flatheads, or wiping down the wrenches, just because my hands and my body need to be doing *something*. So, yeah, no worrying at all. My body feels perfectly fine, except for the fact that it just constantly wants to move. I don't think they have a blood test that shows why my legs want to sprint a marathon at three in the morning, you know? 

I take Uncle Joe to his appointments, obviously. We're at the clinic or the hospital it feels like every other week for his heart or his joints or his blood thinners. And I watch them do all the tests on him—the blood draws, the EKGs, checking his vitals—and I'm usually just standing in the corner of the exam room, shifting my weight from one foot to the other, messing with the zipper on my jacket, just waiting for them to be done so we can get out of there. The nurses sometimes look at me like I'm crazy because I'm practically doing laps around the little rolling stool while they're trying to take his pulse. turns.doctor_question: You mentioned you drink a couple pots of coffee a day while pacing in the kitchen—when you're drinking that much coffee, do you notice the restless feeling gets even worse, or does it feel about the same whether you've had coffee that day or not?
turns.patient_response:
You know, it’s funny you ask about the coffee, because my sister was just telling me the other day—she came over to drop off some groceries, and I was on my, I don't know, maybe my fifth or sixth mug of the morning, just walking circles around the kitchen island while Uncle Joe was watching his game shows in the living room. And she looks at me and says, "You know that stuff is gonna make you jump out of your skin, right?" But honestly? I don't think it makes a lick of difference. I really don't. 

I mean, whether I drink two whole pots of the cheap stuff—I usually get that huge red plastic tub of Folgers, because it's just easier and I go through it so fast—or if I don't have a single drop, that restless feeling, that buzzing in my legs and my chest, it’s exactly the same. It's just always there. Like, there was this one morning last month where we completely ran out, and I couldn't get to the store because the car battery was dead, so I didn't have any coffee at all until like three in the afternoon. And let me tell you, my legs were still doing the exact same tap dance under the table. I was still pacing the exact same worn-out path into the linoleum from the sink to the fridge and back again, just bouncing off the walls the exact same way I always do. 

So, yeah, it doesn't get worse with the coffee. I think I just drink it because it gives my hands something to do, you know? Like, the whole routine of it. Scooping the grounds, pouring the water, watching it drip... it's an activity. It takes up a few minutes. And then holding the warm mug, taking a sip, walking across the room, taking another sip, tapping my fingers on the ceramic... it's just a rhythm. A way to keep moving. 

But as far as the actual jittery, wired feeling inside my body? Nah, the coffee doesn't touch it. It doesn't make it worse, doesn't make it better. My motor is just running at top speed no matter what I put in the tank. I could probably drink a glass of warm milk and I'd still be doing laps around the kitchen table. So to answer your question, no, I haven't noticed it changing anything. It's just... it's just always exactly the same.

turns.doctor_question: When you're deeply focused on something—like watching a movie you really enjoy, or working on fixing your truck—do you still get that same leg bouncing and chest tightness, or does it go away when your mind is occupied?
turns.patient_response:
Well, see, that's the thing. You'd think if I was really into something, my body would just quiet down and let me focus, but... man, I wish it worked like that. It really doesn't. 

Like, if I'm out in the driveway working on my truck—and I love messing with that old Chevy, getting under the hood, trying to figure out why the alternator is whining or whatever—I'll be totally zeroed in on what I'm doing, but my body is still just going, going, going. I'll be tapping the wrench against the fender, or shifting from my left foot to my right foot, kicking the tires, just constantly moving. 

Or movies! Oh man, Uncle Joe loves putting on those old Westerns, the really long ones with John Wayne, and sometimes I actually really want to watch them with him. But I can't just sit there. I'll be staring right at the screen, totally following the plot, but I'll realize I've completely shredded a paper napkin into a hundred tiny little pieces, or I'm bouncing my heel so hard on the floorboards that the whole couch is vibrating and Uncle Joe is giving me the side-eye. 

It actually gets me in trouble sometimes, because people think I'm not paying attention or that I don't care, but I do! Like, take a serious situation. Even when I’m really trying to be respectful—like when we’re at the bank talking to the manager about Uncle Joe’s accounts, or at church, or even sitting right here talking to you—my leg is just bouncing a mile a minute. My fingers are constantly tapping the arm of the chair, or I’m digging in my pockets and finding a receipt or a zip-tie or whatever, and I’m just twisting something in my hands the whole time. 

I can't help it. It's like my brain is locked into the movie or the truck or the conversation, but my body just didn't get the memo that we're supposed to be sitting still. Uncle Joe used to smack my knee when we were in a waiting room or something, telling me to quit shaking the chairs, but I literally don't even realize I'm doing it half the time until somebody points it out. My hands and my legs just have a mind of their own. So, yeah, no matter how much my mind is occupied, the rest of me is still putting on a one-man tap dance. It never stops, Doc. Never.

turns.doctor_question: When you're asleep at night, does your body still move around a lot—like do you wake up and find your sheets all tangled, or does your bed partner ever tell you that you're kicking or thrashing around while you're sleeping? turns.patient_response:
Well, I mean, I don't really know for sure what happens when I'm actually out cold, right? Because, well, I'm asleep. And I don't have a wife or a girlfriend or anybody sharing the mattress with me to, you know, complain about me kicking them or elbowing them in the ribs or whatever. It's just me in that little back bedroom. Uncle Joe's room is all the way down the hall, right next to the bathroom—we put him there because of his bad knees so he doesn't have to walk far in the middle of the night—so he definitely can't hear what I'm doing in my room. 

But I will say, the bed is usually a total disaster zone by the time the sun comes up. I've got this old blue quilt, the heavy kind my mom made years and years ago, and I swear, half the time I wake up and it's completely kicked off the end of the bed onto the floor, or it's twisted around my ankles like a giant pretzel. And the fitted sheet? Forget about it. I have to remake the whole bed every single morning because the corners always pop off. I don't know if they just don't make those pockets deep enough on cheap sheets anymore, or if I'm just in there wrestling an invisible alligator all night. 

But see, the thing is, I don't know if I'm doing all that kicking and tangling when I'm *actually* asleep, or if it's just from the hours I spend tossing and turning trying to get my body to shut down so I *can* fall asleep. Because just laying down in the dark? That's a whole production for me. I'll lay there, and my legs will just be itching to get up and walk down the hall. So I'll flip over to my left side, then two minutes later I flip to my right side, then I roll on my stomach, kick one leg out from under the covers because I feel like I'm burning up, pull it back in because then my foot gets cold... I'm just constantly adjusting and flipping like a burger on a grill. 

So maybe that's what messes up the sheets so bad, just the trying to get to sleep part. But once I actually cross over and I'm snoring? I really couldn't tell you, Doc. Nobody's in there to watch me, and I've never woken myself up from kicking the wall or anything like that. Well, see, that's the whole problem right there. It never really goes away completely. It’s more like... And it makes it practically impossible to just... be normal in places where you're supposed to sit still. 

Like, take supper time with Uncle Joe. He likes to sit at the table, eat his meatloaf or whatever, and just have a quiet meal. A normal person just sits and eats. Not me. I'll take maybe two bites of potatoes, and then I just have to stand up. I’ll tell him I need to get a glass of water. So I get the water, sit back down. Two minutes later, I’m up again, walking over to the front window just to check outside, see if the neighbor's dog got loose or if a car drove by, which is ridiculous because we live on a dead-end street and nobody ever drives by. But I just have to get up and move around. 

And it's not just at home, either. It’s everywhere. If I have to go to a meeting, or like when we were in that waiting room at the Social Security office last month—man, that was a total nightmare. They make you take a number and just sit in those hard plastic chairs for hours. I couldn't do it. I sat down, stood up to go look at the bulletin board. And the whole time, everybody else in the room is just sitting there, totally still, reading magazines or looking at their phones, and they’re all just staring at me. I can see them out of the corner of my eye, giving me these looks like, "What on earth is wrong with this guy?"
